blocks.text: This difficulty was avoided by the late Diodati (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), who renders קפוז kippoz in Italian as gufo, that is, scops [scops-owl]: a bird not only solitary and φιλέρημον [philerēmon], but also nocturnal, ugly and ill-omened, with a harsh and discordant voice ^{(3)}. The old Scholiast of Homer: Σκῶπες· ὄρνεα νυκτίνομα, κακόνομα, κακόφωνα, οἱονεὶ σκαιόπές τινες [Skōpes· ornea nyktinoma, kakonoma, kakophōna, hoionei skaiopes tines]. 2. Add that the name קפוז kippoz, that is, little leaper, seems fitly applicable to a bird that so delights in dancing that, when the fowler dances, it is reported to be caught ἀντορχουμένη [antorchoumenē], that is, dancing in return opposite him. Accordingly Athenaeus ^{e)} counts the scops among the animals which, watching a dancer, νευροσπαστεῖται [neurospasteitai], that is, are moved like puppets νευροσπαστῶν [neurospastōn] (in French des marionettes), and like — a piece of wood moved by another's strings. Hence σκὼψ [skōps] ^{f)} is the name of a kind of dance, notable for its variety of movements and gestures. And σκώπτειν [skōptein] properly means to mimic something with ridiculous imitation, like the scops-owls. 3. Moreover, [col. 411] for scops the ancients mostly wrote cops ^{g)}, without the prefixed Sigma. Among them are Epicharmus, Speusippus, Metrodorus and Alexander of Myndus, who asserts that Homer and Aristotle too wrote κῶπες [kōpes], not σκῶπες [skōpes]. We note this because κῶψ [kōps] comes closer to the Hebrew קפוז kippoz. And the Italian word gufo seems derivable from either, since gli cufi, or gufi, are the copes or scopes of the ancients. Phavorinus: καὶ δοκοῦσι σκῶπες εἶναι, οὓς κούφους ἢ γούφους οἱ Ῥωμαῖοί φασι [kai dokousi skōpes einai, hous kouphous ē gouphous hoi Rhōmaioi phasi]. The same is in Eustathius, except that, instead of κούφους ἢ γούφους [kouphous ē gouphous], our copies wrongly read κουκούβας [koukoubas]. The judicious reader sees that this last interpretation is by far the most probable. Nor, I think, did those mean anything else who rendered the same word eagle-owl, or great owl. Yet this is certain: the scops [III, 198] could not have been called קפוז kippoz because it is ὀρχηστικὴ [orchēstikē] and is caught ἀντορχουμένη [antorchoumenē] by a dancing fowler. For the Hebrew קפז is not ὀρχεῖσθαι [orcheisthai], but ἅλλεσθαι [hallesthai]. We have learned the proper use of the word from the Arabs, who use three nearly synonymous verbs, زج [zj] zaggia, طفر [ṭafara] taphara (in Chaldee טפז tephaz) and قفز [qafaza] kaphaza (in Chaldee קפז kephaz), so interchangeably that زج [zj] zaggia mostly means to leap forward on level ground, طفر [ṭafara] taphara to leap down from a high place to a lower one, قفز [qafaza] kaphaza to leap upward from a lower place. Hence in Avicenna's chapter ^{h)} On the kinds of exercise, القفز [al-qafz] Alcaphzo is done الي شي ليتعلق به [ilā shayʾ li-yataʿallaqa bihi] toward some object, so that one may hang from it. And in the sacred paraphrases قفز [qafaza] kaphaza occurs everywhere for the Hebrew verbs דלג, זנק and נתר, which are known to signify ἅλμα [halma] and πήδημα [pēdēma], not ὄρχησιν [orchēsin]. Therefore קפוז kippoz, if the thing is to answer to the name, must be an animal ἁλτικὸν [haltikon], not ὀρχηστικὸν [orchēstikon] (in French propre a sauter, non a dancer). How much these two differ, everyone sees. Nor was this overlooked by Scaliger, who, explaining the passage of Aristotle where the otus is said to be ἀντορχούμενος [antorchoumenos], History book 8, ch. 12, says: Ἀντορχούμενος [Antorchoumenos], gesticulating in return. Ὄρχησις [Orchēsis] is something other than ἅλμα [halma].
